table.text: The required sample size per arm was approximated by and results were cross-validated against Monte Carlo power estimates derived from (10).
table.header: Vaccine effect, stochastic trial simulation, and operating characteristics

table.text: For example, with a vaccine efficacy of 70%, trials surpass 80% power at sample sizes below 5,000 participants when FoI exceeds 0.05. In contrast, in low-transmission settings (e.g., λ = 0.01), even large cohorts of 50,000 participants may remain underpowered. Figure 5 displays the Bayesian posterior distribution of vaccine efficacy. Using weakly informative priors, the posterior mean of vaccine efficacy aligns closely with the true simulated value of 70%. The 95% credible interval ranges from 0.68 to 0.71, reflecting statistical uncertainty due to sample size limitations and variability in event rates.

Figure 9: Statistical power as a function of force of infection (FoI) for different sample sizes per trial arm, assuming 70% vaccine efficacy. Even at the largest simulated sample size (5,000 participants per arm), power remains below 30% when FoI is between 0.01 and 0.03, reflecting typical dengue transmission levels in many endemic regions. Smaller sample sizes (500 to 2,000) result in even lower power, highlighting the operational challenges of conducting dengue vaccine trials in low-transmission settings.

Figure 4: Power curves generated across varying force of infection (FoI) levels and vaccine efficacy (VE). Solid lines represent 70% VE, while dashed lines represent 50% VE. Different colors correspond to varying sample sizes (500, 2000, 5000 participants per arm). Higher FoI values substantially reduce the sample size required to achieve 80% power.

In low-transmission settings, where FoI ranges between 0.01 and 0.03-representing typical epidemiological conditions in many dengue-endemic regions-the statistical power remains below 30%, even when enrolling 5,000 participants per arm. This reflects a significant risk of Type II error, whereby the trial may fail to detect a true vaccine effect due to insufficient case accrual. Smaller trials with 500 to 2,000 participants per arm perform even worse, often yielding power below 10-20%. These findings highlight the substantial challenge of conducting dengue vaccine trials in low-transmission environments, where symptomatic events are rare.
As the FoI increases toward 0.05 and beyond, the statistical power improves sharply, with trials surpassing the 80% power threshold needed for reliable hypothesis testing.

text.text: Dengue fever, transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti, remains a major global public health threat, causing an estimated 390 million infections annually.

Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral disease caused by four antigenically distinct dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4).
It is an expanding global public health challenge, with an estimated 390 million infections each year and roughly 96 million clinically apparent cases [1].
text.formatted: It is an expanding global public health challenge, with an estimated 390 million infections each year and roughly 96 million clinically apparent cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The virus is transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti, a vector that thrives in warm and humid environments and is strongly influenced by urbanization, climate variability, and human mobility [2, 3].
text.formatted: The virus is transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti, a vector that thrives in warm and humid environments and is strongly influenced by urbanization, climate variability, and human mobility <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: Clinical presentation ranges from mild febrile illness to severe disease, including dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome, contributing to substantial morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality in many endemic settings [4]..
text.formatted: Clinical presentation ranges from mild febrile illness to severe disease, including dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome, contributing to substantial morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality in many endemic settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>..

text.text: The frequency and geographic range of dengue outbreaks have increased substantially in recent decades, driven by climate change, rapid urbanization, population mobility, and persistent limitations in vector control and surveillance systems.

Climate variability influences rainfall patterns and increases ambient temperatures, thereby expanding the seasonal window and geographic suitability for Aedes mosquito breeding and dengue transmission [5] [6] [7]..
text.formatted: Climate variability influences rainfall patterns and increases ambient temperatures, thereby expanding the seasonal window and geographic suitability for Aedes mosquito breeding and dengue transmission <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[7]</ref>..

text.text: At the same time, limitations in public health infrastructure and routine surveillance can delay outbreak detection and response, increasing community vulnerability.

Dengue is increasingly recognized as an emerging public health concern in Africa, although the true burden is likely underestimated due to limited diagnostic capacity, misclassification with other febrile illnesses, and incomplete surveillance and reporting systems [8] [9] [10].
text.formatted: Dengue is increasingly recognized as an emerging public health concern in Africa, although the true burden is likely underestimated due to limited diagnostic capacity, misclassification with other febrile illnesses, and incomplete surveillance and reporting systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Such dynamics underscore the need for robust and scalable prevention strategies, including vaccines and complementary interventions.

Despite the availability of licensed dengue vaccines and the continued development of additional candidates, the design and implementation of vaccine efficacy trials remain challenging [11] [12] [13] [14].

text.text: Dengue transmission exhibits pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity, with infection risk varying substantially between communities and fluctuating across seasons, which complicates site selection and often results in slowerthan-anticipated endpoint accrual and underpowered studies [15, 38].

text.text: Building on this logic, the present study develops a mathematical simulation framework for dengue trial design in endemic settings that (i) links FoI to age-specific seroprevalence, (ii) represents baseline population immunity in trial cohorts, and (iii) simulates randomized controlled trials under varying FoI, vaccine efficacy, and follow-up assumptions to quantify sample size and power requirements.
This work is intended to provide theoretical, scenario-based guidance for trial planning rather than empirical predictions of vaccine impact at a specific location.
The analyses rely on model-based assumptions to enable controlled experimentation across a wide range of plausible endemic conditions.

Accordingly, results should be interpreted as design-oriented insights that highlight feasibility thresholds and the relative importance of transmission intensity, baseline immunity, and surveillance detection.

The remainder of the manuscript presents the modeling framework, simulation procedures, and sensitivity analyses, and discusses implications for sample size determination, follow-up planning, and site selection in dengue-endemic regions.

Dengue vaccine efficacy trials are typically conducted in endemic settings, where a substantial proportion of the population has prior exposure to dengue virus and baseline immunity is heterogeneous across age groups [13, 28, 29].

text.text: Under such conditions, the accumulation of trial endpoints is primarily determined by the local force of infection (FoI) rather than by short-term epidemic dynamics in a fully susceptible population.
Accordingly, the present study adopts a FoI-based framework to evaluate trial feasibility.

Infection risk and symptomatic endpoints were generated directly from assumed FoI values, and operating characteristics of candidate trial designs were assessed across a range of epidemiologically realistic scenarios.
The analytical framework consisted of four sequential and internally linked components.
First, the relationship between FoI and age-specific seroprevalence was established using a catalytic model under endemic equilibrium assumptions.
This step provided a consistent epidemiological basis for translating transmission intensity into observable population immunity patterns.

Second, the same catalytic relationship was used to represent baseline immunity within the trial-eligible population, ensuring that simulated cohorts reflected realistic levels of pre-existing exposure.
Third, FoI was converted into symptomatic disease incidence, which served as the primary endpoint risk in simulated vaccine and placebo arms.
Trial outcomes were then generated under specified assumptions regarding vaccine efficacy, follow-up duration, and case detection.

Finally, statistical power and required sample sizes were evaluated across predefined grids of FoI, vaccine efficacy, and follow-up time to identify design configurations capable of achieving adequate operating characteristics under different transmission settings.
To provide epidemiological context, a mechanistic vector-host transmission model based on an SEIR-SEI structure was also implemented.
Such models are widely used to represent dengue transmission dynamics and to evaluate the effects of vector control and behavioral or ecological factors on disease spread [30] [31] [32].

This section presents the outcomes of the dengue vaccine trial simulations and modelbased analyses.
We report on the estimated sample size requirements, power curves, and case accrual projections under varying epidemiological scenarios.

The results further include Bayesian posterior estimates of vaccine efficacy, sensitivity analyses across force of infection (FoI) and symptomatic disease probabilities, and validation metrics comparing simulated outputs to empirical data.
Collectively, these findings provide a comprehensive framework for informing trial design, site selection, and policy decisions in dengue-endemic settings.

From a trial design perspective, these findings have clear implications.
Site selection should prioritize high-transmission areas to ensure adequate RD and timely endpoint accrual, and pre-trial FoI mapping is essential.

In low-transmission settings, achieving sufficient statistical power will require either substantially larger sample sizes, extended follow-up periods, or the use of serological endpoints to increase event counts.

Finally, the anticipated vaccine efficacy must be carefully balanced against the local FoI; higher VE reduces observed event rates in the vaccine arm, which can risk underpowering the study if the underlying transmission intensity is low.

The results highlight that endpoint accrual and thus statistical power is driven pri-marily by transmission intensity (FoI), while vaccine efficacy modulates, but does not fundamentally alter, this relationship.

Consequently, strategic site selection, realistic assumptions about VE, and careful alignment of sample size requirements with local FoI estimates are critical to the feasibility and success of dengue vaccine trials.

text.text: The results show a pronounced inverse relationship between FoI and required sample size: as FoI increases, the number of participants needed declines sharply.
For example, when FoI is below 0.03, the required sample size can exceed several thousand participants per arm, making trial implementation logistically complex and financially burdensome.
Conversely, in high-transmission settings (FoI above 0.08), the required sample size drops substantially, reflecting faster endpoint accrual.
Trials designed for higher VE thresholds consistently require fewer participants due to larger anticipated effect sizes, further improving feasibility.
These findings underscore the critical role of accurate FoI estimation in trial planning and highlight the potential efficiency gains from selecting sites with higher baseline transmission.

text.text: The results demonstrate that the probability of successfully detecting a vaccine effect depends critically on both the underlying transmission intensity and the sample size allocated to each trial group.

In low-transmission settings, where FoI ranges between 0.01 and 0.03-representing typical epidemiological conditions in many dengue-endemic regions-the statistical power remains below 30%, even when enrolling 5,000 participants per arm.
This reflects a significant risk of Type II error, whereby the trial may fail to detect a true vaccine effect due to insufficient case accrual.
Smaller trials with 500 to 2,000 participants per arm perform even worse, often yielding power below 10-20%.
These findings highlight the substantial challenge of conducting dengue vaccine trials in low-transmission environments, where symptomatic events are rare.
As the FoI increases toward 0.05 and beyond, the statistical power improves sharply, with trials surpassing the 80% power threshold needed for reliable hypothesis testing.
This confirms that conducting trials in high-transmission settings is both more efficient and feasible, as more cases accumulate rapidly, reducing the required sample size and follow-up duration.

Site selection emerges as a critical determinant of trial success; vaccine trials should prioritize high-endemicity areas where transmission is ongoing, maximizing the likelihood of accruing sufficient clinical endpoints.
In low-transmission settings, alternative trial designs may be necessary, including the use of surrogate endpoints such as seroconversion or extending the follow-up period.

Seroprevalence steadily increases with age, reaching near-universal exposure in older adults.

These findings suggest that children and young adults (ages 4-11) are the optimal target populations for dengue vaccine trials due to their higher rates of primary infection and greater susceptibility to clinical disease.

The simulation results illustrate the rapid spread of dengue fever within a closed population of 10,000 humans interacting with a mosquito population of 30,000, revealing the intricate interplay between host and vector populations in sustaining transmission.
This study demonstrates the pivotal role of the local epidemiological context in the design and implementation of dengue vaccine trials.
The feasibility and success of such trials depend on the dynamic interplay between the force of infection (FoI), baseline disease incidence, vaccine efficacy assumptions, and required sample sizes.
Simulation results show that low-transmission settings often lead to slow case accrual, underpowered analyses, and increased operational costs.
In contrast, medium-to-high FoI environments facilitate more rapid endpoint generation, reduce sample size demands, and enhance overall trial efficiency.

From a practical standpoint, these findings highlight the necessity of integrating mathematical modeling particularly FoI estimation and Bayesian uncertainty quantification into the early stages of clinical trial planning.

Such integration enables sponsors, policymakers, and public health planners to identify optimal trial sites, anticipate logistical requirements, and align study designs with realistic transmission expectations.

By tailoring vaccine trials to the local epidemiological profile, researchers can maximize resource efficiency, minimize trial duration, and enhance the likelihood of obtaining conclusive and generalizable results.
Ultimately, this modeling-informed approach strengthens evidencebased decision-making and supports accelerated, context-sensitive deployment of dengue vaccines in endemic regions.
However, it is important to acknowledge that these conclusions are derived primarily from simulated epidemiological scenarios without direct field validation.
Although simulation models offer flexibility to explore diverse transmission conditions and programmatic strategies, they cannot fully capture the complexity of real-world dengue transmission.
Variations in vector ecology, climatic patterns, human mobility, heterogeneous immunity, and socio-environmental dynamics may lead to outcomes that differ from model projections.

Moreover, several assumptions underpinning the model-including closed population structures, homogeneous mixing, fixed demographic patterns, and literature-based vaccine efficacy parameters-were necessary for tractability but may limit generalizability across settings.
For these reasons, the findings should be interpreted as methodological guidance to support trial planning rather than as empirical predictions of vaccine impact.

Future work should therefore incorporate primary field data, strengthen model calibration and validation procedures, integrate spatial heterogeneity, and explore adaptive trial designs aligned with observed transmission patterns.

Such enhancements will improve predictive accuracy, increase operational relevance, and ultimately expand the value of modeling frameworks in guiding the development, evaluation, and deployment of dengue vaccines.

Figure1illustrates the results of the SEIR-SEI transmission model simulation over a two-year period, capturing the dynamic interplay between human hosts and mosquito vectors in dengue virus transmission.
The number of susceptible human individuals (S H ) declines sharply during the first year of the simulation, reflecting intense transmission pressure.

Correspondingly, the exposed (E H ) and infectious (I H ) compartments exhibit a classical epidemic trajectory, rising rapidly, peaking at the height of transmission, and subsequently declining as individuals transition into the recovered class (R H ).
By the end of the two-year simulation period, fewer than 1% of individuals remain susceptible, and approximately 99% of the population has experienced at least one infection.

This pattern represents a scenario of near-complete infection saturation driven by sustained vector-mediated transmission.The mosquito population sustains transmission during the growth phase of the epidemic.

Susceptible mosquitoes (S V ) initially decline as vectors acquire infection from infectious humans through the force of infection λ V (t) defined in Appendix A. Infected mosquitoes progress from the exposed (E V ) to the infectious (I V ) state and remain infectious for life.As human infections decline, the force of infection on mosquitoes decreases, leading to fewer newly infected vectors.
At the same time, demographic turnover continuously replenishes the mosquito population with newly emerged susceptible individuals at rate µ V N V .
This demographic replacement explains the observed rebound in the susceptible mosquito population during the later stages of the simulation.

Importantly, because mosquito infection depends entirely on infectious humans, the infectious mosquito popu-lation declines progressively as human infection approaches zero.In this closed-population framework, the long-term equilibrium of the system is diseasefree in both hosts and vectors.
Once human infections disappear, no new mosquito infections occur, and the infectious vector population declines to zero due to mortality.

Consequently, sustained transmission cannot re-emerge without the reintroduction of infection into either the human or mosquito population.The simulation highlights the strong coupling between human and vector dynamics during the epidemic growth phase and illustrates the process of immunity saturation in the human population.
However, it is important to emphasize that this mechanistic SEIR-SEI model is presented for conceptual illustration only.

During the first year, the number of susceptible humans (S H ) declines sharply, reaching approximately 99% infection saturation.

This follows the classical epidemic curve, where exposed (E H ) and infectious (I H ) compartments rise, peak, and subsequently decline as individuals transition into the recovered (R H ) class, reflecting the accumulation of immunity.
In contrast, the mosquito population remains infectious throughout the simulation since mosquitoes do not recover.
Instead, they transition from exposed (E V ) to infectious (I V ) states until death, maintaining a reservoir for viral persistence.

This finding underscores the critical role of mosquitoes as both vectors and reservoirs of dengue, consistent with previous work emphasizing the need for integrated approaches combining vaccination, antiviral therapy, and vector control (Alnoor et al., 2025; Medeiros et al., 2011; Martheswaran et al., 2020).
The persistent infectious mosquito population highlights the potential for transmission to continue even when human immunity is widespread.
Our findings extend earlier studies by showing that, despite high human seroprevalence, the continual turnover of mosquitoes enables the virus to persist in the environment.
This suggests that control strategies focusing solely on human immunity are insufficient without addressing the continuous replenishment of susceptible vectors.

Similar conclusions have been drawn in recent modeling studies demonstrating that the effectiveness of vaccination and vector control depends strongly on demographic and epidemiological contexts (Djaafara et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2022; Khan et al., 2025).
The relationship between the force of infection (FoI), disease incidence, and seroprevalence provides important insight into dengue transmission and vaccine trial feasibility.
As FoI increases, the proportion of infected individuals and overall seroprevalence also rise, aligning with both simulated and empirical findings (Tan et al., 2019; Carrera et al., 2020).
At moderate FoI levels (e.g., 0.05 per person-year), infection risk reaches roughly 60%, illustrating the direct dependence of cumulative exposure on transmission intensity.

Younger populations exhibit a slower rise in disease incidence due to limited cumulative exposure, whereas older populations approach earlier plateaus in infection risk due to prior immunity (Annan et al., 2023; Thai et al., 2011; Kumar et al., 2020).

These patterns demonstrate that age and prior exposure significantly influence both infection dynamics and clinical outcomes, supporting age-targeted intervention strategies (Nealon et al., 2022; Phuong et al., 2024).
Age-specific attack rates derived from the simulation confirm these relationships.

The highest attack rates occurred among the 0-4 and 20-24 year age groups (43% and 47%, respectively), reflecting both early-life vulnerability and cumulative adult exposure (Dhar-Chowdhury et al., 2017; Biggs et al., 2021).
This bimodal distribution indicates that while children are at high risk due to lack of prior exposure, young adults remain vulnerable due to increased contact rates and occupational exposure.

Consequently, both demographic structure and age distribution must be considered when designing vaccine trials and evaluating public health interventions.The FoI further determines the feasibility of vaccine trials by influencing endpoint accrual and statistical power.

Low-transmission settings often produce underpowered results and require longer follow-up, while medium-to-high FoI environments facilitate faster case accrual and more efficient trial execution(Mueller et al., 2012; Li et al., 2019;Kaslow, 2021).

Integrating demographic heterogeneity, prior exposure history, and agespecific susceptibility into vaccine trial design is therefore critical for accurate efficacy estimation and realistic impact assessment (Madewell et al., 2021).

Regions with younger populations are likely to experience higher outbreak risks due to lower baseline immunity, whereas older populations may achieve faster saturation, reducing susceptibility to reinfection.
These demographic variations should guide vaccine trial size, duration, and design to ensure context-appropriate and efficient implementation.
